title: Parity Floors in Quantum Denoisers: A Closed-Form Benchmark for Fixed-Map Denoising Networks
abstract: Fixed quantum feature maps are increasingly inserted into diffusion denoisers, but standard image benchmarks do not reveal which structural constraint limits them. We introduce CoupledPhaseTexture, a torus-diffusion benchmark with analytic heat-kernel noising that separates parity, within-sector approximation, and sample-complexity limitations. For the depth-1 RY+CNOT+Pauli-Z family we prove a containment-free parity floor: all reachable features are even functions of the encoded angles while the sine components of the Bayes denoiser are odd, so the excess risk splits exactly into an inaccessible odd part and a within-sector residual. The first term is an irreducible, noise-scale-resolved lower bound holding for every even feature class, with no containment, linearity, or closedness assumption on the feature class. The obstruction is a property of the noise-conditioned denoising target rather than static representability: the floor is re-derived at each noise scale because the target's parity content changes with noise. The measured excess is dominated by the parity proxy on two distinct priors. Higher-order Z readouts improve the even sector, but entanglement does not lower the floor and re-uploading does not reliably close it. Classical controls confirm the deficit is parity rather than quantumness: a cosine-only bank is floored similarly, while adding the sine sector matches the reference. Among tested constructions, odd readouts and a noise-coupled encoder do not match the sine-carrying classical bank. These results motivate nonclassical data access or feature classes without efficient classical surrogates; they do not establish either as sufficient for quantum advantage.
summary: This work introduces a novel benchmark to analyze fixed quantum feature maps used in diffusion denoisers. By decomposing the reconstruction error into even and odd components, the authors prove that the primary limitation (the 'parity floor') is dictated by the target's odd spectral content rather than the map's ability to represent all features. This guides future research toward nonclassical data access methods.
main_problem: The study aims to determine which structural constraint limits fixed quantum feature maps when used within diffusion denoisers, distinguishing between representational limitations and other sources of error.
main_result: The excess risk in the denoising process is shown to be dominated by an irreducible 'parity floor,' which is a property of the noise-conditioned target rather than static map capacity.
method: The authors develop a closed-form benchmark using analytic heat-kernel noising on a torus, decomposing the excess risk into parity and within-sector residual components based on even/odd subspaces.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum feature maps (e.g., depth-1 RY+CNOT+Pauli-Z) applied to a diffusion process defined by a Gibbs law prior on the torus ($\mathbb{T}^n$).
key_observables: Excess risk, parity proxy ($\hat{P}_\sigma$), signed empirical residual ($\hat{\delta}_{\sigma,N}$), and the irreducible lower bound $\|\Pi_{	ext{odd}}m_\sigma\|^2$.
important_parameters: Noise scale ($\sigma$), feature map depth, and the structure of the prior (e.g., 3-body coupling on $\mathbb{T}^n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the excess risk can be decomposed into parity and within-sector components; the results are limited to fixed feature maps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how quantum excess tracks the calculated parity proxy across varying noise levels, confirming parity dominance over capacity limitations.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes a theoretical decomposition of the risk based on even/odd subspaces. It then applies this framework to specific fixed quantum feature map families (depth-1) and compares performance against classical benchmarks using various priors (torus, signed-XY).
why_interesting: It provides rigorous mathematical tools for diagnosing fundamental limitations in variational quantum algorithms applied to physical processes like diffusion modeling, suggesting that parity constraints are a more fundamental barrier than simple model capacity.
